sections.title: Start here
sections.body:
Fluids at rest press equally in all directions, and the pressure grows with depth. Fluids in motion trade pressure, speed and height against each other while keeping the total the same, apart from losses.

Two ideas carry most questions: what goes in must come out, and energy is conserved along the flow.
pitfalls: Using pipe diameter where the formula needs area: area changes with the square of diameter.

tips.from: Mark Mattson, FE Fluid Mechanics Review Session 2022
items: Decide at the start whether the question wants gauge or absolute pressure.
Work through a manometer in one direction, adding pressure going down and subtracting going up, and do not change direction partway.
The force on a submerged surface can be checked with statics: draw the pressure diagram, split it into a rectangle and a triangle, and take their areas.
In the centre of pressure formula, the dimension that is cubed in the moment of inertia is the one measured down the surface.
For a jet turned by a vane, find the force components separately with the cosine and sine of the turning angle.

bridge.plain: Fluid mechanics describes water and other fluids at rest and in motion. At rest, pressure grows with depth. In motion, a fluid trades pressure, speed and height against each other, and loses some energy to friction.
core: Flow rate = velocity × area, and it is the same at every section of a full pipe.
The energy equation tracks pressure, speed and elevation, minus losses, along the flow.
A fluid that changes speed or direction pushes on whatever turns it.
bridge.links: Water resources applies it to pipes, pumps, channels and drains. Geotechnics uses the pressure ideas for groundwater. Statics supplies the force and centroid methods.
bridge.exam: Fluid mechanics has its own handbook chapter; open-channel formulas also appear in the civil chapter.

sections.title: Flow measurement
sections.body:
Flow meters work by making the fluid trade pressure for speed and then measuring the pressure change. A Pitot tube points into the flow and stops a small stream of it; the extra pressure it reads is the velocity head. A venturi and an orifice plate squeeze the flow through a smaller opening and measure the pressure drop across it.

Real meters lose a little energy and the jet narrows, so a discharge coefficient below 1 corrects the ideal answer. Weirs measure open-channel flow from the height of water over a crest.
pitfalls: Using diameter where area is needed.

example.problem: A tank drains through a 20 mm hole 2 m below the water surface with a discharge coefficient of 0.62. Find the flow in L/s.

ideas.title: What a Pitot tube measures
ideas.text: Water stalls at the mouth of the tube, so its velocity head turns into extra height in the column. The difference between the stagnation and static columns is v^{2} / 2g, and the handbook's Pitot formula is Bernoulli's equation already solved for v.

ideas.title: One reading is not the mean
ideas.text: Flow is slower near the bed and walls, so a single velocity measured mid-stream overstates the mean. A correction factor, or several readings, is needed before multiplying by area.

ideas.title: Orifice coefficients
ideas.text: The discharge coefficient combines contraction of the jet and friction. For a sharp-edged orifice it is about 0.61. The handbook table is listed under the orifice's description, such as sharp-edged or submerged.

ideas.title: Pitot tube
ideas.text: At the tip of a Pitot tube the flow is brought to rest and its velocity head, V^{2} / 2g, is converted to pressure head. The difference between stagnation and static head is therefore the velocity head.

ideas.title: Orifice
ideas.text: Torricelli's result gives the ideal jet velocity as the square root of 2 g h. Real flow is smaller because of jet contraction and friction, which the discharge coefficient accounts for: Q = C_{d} A × square root of (2 g h).

examples.problem: A Pitot tube in a water stream shows a stagnation head 0.60 m higher than the static head. What is the flow velocity? Use g = 9.81 m/s^{2}.
examples.idea: At the tip of a Pitot tube the flow is brought to rest and its velocity head, V^{2} / 2g, is converted to pressure head. The difference between stagnation and static head is therefore the velocity head.

examples.problem: Water discharges through a 60 mm diameter orifice under a head of 4 m. The discharge coefficient is 0.61. What is the flow rate? Use g = 9.81 m/s^{2}.
examples.idea: Torricelli's result gives the ideal jet velocity as the square root of 2 g h. Real flow is smaller because of jet contraction and friction, which the discharge coefficient accounts for: Q = C_{d} A × square root of (2 g h).

examples.problem: A venturi meter in a 225 mm water pipe has a 120 mm throat. The piezometric head drops by 0.8 m between inlet and throat, and the meter coefficient is 0.98. What is the flow rate? Use g = 9.81 m/s^{2}.
examples.idea: A venturi speeds the flow up in its throat, and Bernoulli's equation turns the resulting drop in head into a velocity. Continuity brings in the area ratio: Q = C_{v} A_{2} × square root of (2 g × head drop / (1 - (A_{2}/A_{1})^{2})).

figure.svg: <path d='M30 40 L170 40 L230 58 L370 58 L370 92 L230 92 L170 110 L30 110 Z' fill='#568CBB' fill-opacity='.25' stroke='#00242E' stroke-width='2'/><line x1='60' y1='75' x2='110' y2='75' stroke='#00574A' stroke-width='3'/><path d='M118 75 L104 69 L104 81 Z' fill='#00574A'/><text x='100' y='30' text-anchor='middle' font-size='12' font-weight='400' fill='#00242E'>225 mm</text><text x='300' y='48' text-anchor='middle' font-size='12' font-weight='400' fill='#00242E'>120 mm</text><text x='100' y='130' text-anchor='middle' font-size='12' font-weight='400' fill='#00242E'>Section 1</text><text x='300' y='112' text-anchor='middle' font-size='12' font-weight='400' fill='#00242E'>Section 2</text>

examples.problem: A 90° V-notch weir has a head of 0.28 m above the bottom of the notch. Using Q = 1.40 H^{5/2} in SI units, what is the discharge?
examples.idea: Flow through a triangular notch grows with the head to the 5/2 power, because both the depth and the width of the flow section increase with head. That makes a V-notch sensitive at low flows.

examples.problem: An orifice plate with a 58 mm opening and a discharge coefficient of 0.62 is installed in a water line. The pressure drop across it is 34 kPa. What is the flow rate? Take the density of water as 1,000 kg/m^{3} and ignore the approach velocity.
examples.idea: An orifice turns pressure into velocity: the ideal velocity is the square root of (2 × pressure drop / density). The discharge coefficient allows for the contraction of the jet and for friction.

sections.deep:
Flow is measured by making the fluid change speed and reading the pressure change that results, which is Bernoulli's equation put to work. A Pitot tube brings the flow to rest and reads the velocity head. Venturi meters, nozzles and orifice plates contract the flow and read the pressure drop, with a coefficient that corrects for losses and contraction.

In open channels, weirs relate the head over the crest to discharge: a rectangular weir's flow varies with head to the 3/2 power and a V-notch weir's with head to the 5/2 power. A free orifice discharges at the coefficient times area times the square root of 2 g h.
method: Identify the device and find its equation in the handbook.
Compute the area of the throat, orifice or crest.
Convert pressure differences to head of the flowing fluid.
Check units, especially mm to m in areas.
sections.credit: Some of the points in this lesson follow Mark Mattson's 2022 FE review session for this topic, restated in this site's words.
sections.primer: Flow is measured by making the fluid do something that can be read. A narrowing speeds the flow up and lowers its pressure; a weir makes water spill over at a depth that depends on the flow. Each device has a formula that turns the reading into a flow rate.

terms: head
energy of a fluid expressed as a height of that fluid, in metres or feet
symbols: head: energy per unit weight of fluid, as a height

sections.title: Fluid properties
sections.body:
Density is mass per volume. Specific weight is weight per volume, which is density times gravity. Specific gravity compares a fluid's density with water's.

Viscosity is a fluid's resistance to flowing: honey has a high viscosity and water a low one. Dynamic viscosity links shear stress to how fast one layer slides over the next. Kinematic viscosity is dynamic viscosity divided by density. The Reynolds number compares inertia with viscosity and tells you whether pipe flow is smooth (laminar, below about 2,100) or churning (turbulent).
pitfalls: Confusing dynamic and kinematic viscosity. Check the units: Pa·s versus m^{2}/s.

example.problem: Oil with a kinematic viscosity of 4 × 10^{-5} m^{2}/s flows at 0.8 m/s in a 50 mm pipe. Is the flow laminar?
example.steps:
Re = \frac{0.8(0.05)}{4 × 10^{-5}} = 1,000.

That is below 2,100, so the flow is laminar.

ideas.title: Numbers to know
ideas.text: Water: 1,000 kg/m^{3}, 9,810 N/m^{3}, 62.4 lb/ft^{3}. Specific weight divided by density is g. A density in g/mL times 1,000 is in kg/m^{3}.

ideas.title: Specific gravity
ideas.text: Specific gravity is the ratio of a liquid's density (or specific weight) to that of water. Multiply by the specific weight of water to get the liquid's specific weight.

ideas.title: Reynolds number
ideas.text: The Reynolds number is the ratio of inertial to viscous forces: Re = V D / (kinematic viscosity). In pipes, flow is laminar below about 2,100 and turbulent above about 4,000, which decides how the friction factor is found.

ideas.title: Kinematic viscosity
ideas.text: Kinematic viscosity is dynamic viscosity divided by density. It is the form that appears in the Reynolds number.

examples.problem: A liquid has a specific gravity of 0.88. What is its specific weight? Use 9.81 kN/m^{3} for water.
examples.idea: Specific gravity is the ratio of a liquid's density (or specific weight) to that of water. Multiply by the specific weight of water to get the liquid's specific weight.

examples.problem: Water flows at 2.5 m/s in a 200 mm diameter pipe. Its kinematic viscosity is 1.0 × 10^{-6} m^{2}/s. What is the Reynolds number?
examples.idea: The Reynolds number is the ratio of inertial to viscous forces: Re = V D / (kinematic viscosity). In pipes, flow is laminar below about 2,100 and turbulent above about 4,000, which decides how the friction factor is found.
examples.steps: Re = \frac{V D}{kinematic viscosity} = \frac{2.5(0.200)}{1.0 × 10^{-6}} = 500,000, which is turbulent.

examples.problem: A liquid has a dynamic viscosity of 0.0018 Pa·s and a density of 900 kg/m^{3}. What is its kinematic viscosity? Give the answer in units of 10^{-6} m^{2}/s.
examples.idea: Kinematic viscosity is dynamic viscosity divided by density. It is the form that appears in the Reynolds number.

examples.problem: A clean glass tube with an inside diameter of 1.5 mm stands in water. The surface tension is 0.0728 N/m and the contact angle is 0°. How high does the water rise in the tube? Use 9,810 N/m^{3} for water.
examples.idea: Surface tension pulling up around the tube's wall supports the weight of the raised column: h = 4 (surface tension) cos(contact angle) / (specific weight × diameter). Narrower tubes give a higher rise.

examples.problem: A flat plate with an area of 0.12 m^{2} slides at 0.4 m/s over a fixed surface on an oil film 1.0 mm thick. The oil's dynamic viscosity is 0.64 Pa·s. What force keeps the plate moving?
examples.idea: For a thin film the velocity varies linearly across the gap, so the shear stress is viscosity times velocity divided by film thickness (Newton's law of viscosity). Force is stress times area.

figure.alt: Free-body diagram showing Pull = 30.7 N, Oil drag.

examples.problem: A sample weighs 63.8 N in air and 39.9 N when fully submerged in water. What is its specific gravity?
examples.idea: The loss of weight in water equals the weight of water displaced, which has the sample's volume. Specific gravity is therefore the weight in air divided by the loss of weight.

sections.deep:
Fluid properties describe how a fluid responds to forces. Density is mass per volume, specific weight is weight per volume (density times g) and specific gravity is the ratio to water. Viscosity is resistance to shearing: dynamic viscosity relates shear stress to velocity gradient, and kinematic viscosity is dynamic viscosity divided by density.

Other properties appear less often: surface tension causes capillary rise, vapour pressure sets the onset of cavitation and bulk modulus measures compressibility. Water is treated as incompressible in nearly all exam problems.
method: Write down which property is given and which is wanted.
Use specific weight = density × g and specific gravity = density / density of water to convert.
For viscosity conversions, divide dynamic by density to get kinematic.
Keep to one unit system throughout.
sections.credit: Some of the points in this lesson follow Mark Mattson's 2022 FE review session for this topic, restated in this site's words.
sections.primer: Fluid properties say how heavy and how thick a fluid is. Density is mass per volume; specific weight is weight per volume; specific gravity compares the density with water's. Viscosity measures resistance to flowing.
leads: Water Resources and Environmental Engineering: Groundwater
terms: specific weight
weight per unit volume; for water 9.81 kN/m^{3} or 62.4 lb/ft^{3}
specific gravity
density of a substance divided by the density of water; it has no units
viscosity
a fluid's resistance to flowing; honey has a high viscosity, water a low one
shear stress
force per unit area acting parallel to a surface, trying to slide one layer over the next
reynolds number
a ratio that tells whether flow is smooth (laminar, low values) or mixed and eddying (turbulent, high values)
laminar
smooth, layered flow with no mixing between layers
symbols: acceleration due to gravity, 9.81 m/s^{2} (32.2 ft/s^{2})

sections.title: Fluid statics
sections.body:
In a fluid at rest, pressure depends only on depth and acts equally in all directions. It increases by the specific weight for every unit of depth. Gauge pressure is measured from atmospheric; absolute pressure includes the atmosphere.

A manometer reads pressure as the height of a liquid column: move through it adding pressure going down and subtracting going up. The force on a submerged flat surface equals the pressure at the surface's centroid times its area, and it acts below the centroid. A floating or submerged body is pushed up by a force equal to the weight of fluid it displaces.
pitfalls: Using the depth to the top of a surface instead of the depth to its centroid.
Mixing gauge and absolute pressures in one equation.
In the centre of pressure formula, dividing I by y_{c} alone. It is divided by the product y_{c} A.

example.problem: Find the gauge pressure at the bottom of a 5 m deep tank of oil with a specific gravity of 0.9.

figure.alt: A vertical gate 3 m tall and 2 m wide with its top at the water surface and a triangular pressure diagram.
figure.caption: Hydrostatic pressure on a vertical gate grows linearly with depth. The resultant acts at two thirds of the depth.

ideas.title: Layered liquids
ideas.text: Pressure at depth is the sum of density × g × thickness for each layer above. The pressure diagram for a lower layer starts at the pressure of the interface, not at zero.

ideas.title: Force on a wall from the pressure diagram
ideas.text: The force on a vertical wall is the area of its pressure diagram times the wall's width. Split the diagram into rectangles and triangles; a triangle's resultant acts two thirds of the way down from its apex.

ideas.title: Centre of pressure on an inclined surface
ideas.text: Measure along the slope: y_{cp} = y_{c} + I / (y_{c} A), with the moment of inertia taken for the dimension that runs down the slope. Convert between vertical depth and slant distance with the sine of the angle. The shift below the centroid is small for a small gate at depth.

ideas.title: Barometers and floating loads
ideas.text: A barometer column balances atmospheric pressure: p = specific weight × height. A raft can carry a load equal to the weight of water it could displace minus its own weight.

ideas.title: Pressure field in a static liquid
ideas.text: In a fluid at rest, pressure increases linearly with depth: p = (specific weight) × h. Gauge pressure is measured relative to the atmosphere, so it is zero at the free surface.

ideas.title: Forces on submerged surfaces
ideas.text: The resultant force on a submerged plane surface is the pressure at the centroid of the area times the area. For a gate that reaches the surface the pressure diagram is a triangle, and the force acts at two thirds of the depth.

ideas.title: Manometer
ideas.text: Work around the manometer from one pipe to the other, adding pressure going down and subtracting going up. The water columns on the two sides cancel except over the deflection, leaving (SG of mercury - 1) × specific weight of water × deflection.

ideas.title: Buoyancy
ideas.text: Archimedes' principle: a floating body displaces a weight of fluid equal to its own weight. In water, the submerged fraction of the volume equals the body's specific gravity.

ideas.title: Pressure field in a static liquid
ideas.text: Pressure at depth is the sum of specific weight times thickness for each layer above. The lower layer starts from the pressure at the interface, not from zero.

ideas.title: Buoyancy
ideas.text: At the limit the raft is fully submerged and displaces its whole volume of water. The buoyant force then equals the raft's weight plus the cargo, so the cargo is the weight of displaced water minus the weight of the raft.

examples.problem: What is the gauge pressure 15 m below the surface of a freshwater reservoir? Use a specific weight of 9.81 kN/m^{3}.
examples.idea: In a fluid at rest, pressure increases linearly with depth: p = (specific weight) × h. Gauge pressure is measured relative to the atmosphere, so it is zero at the free surface.

examples.problem: A vertical rectangular gate is 2.5 m wide and 3.6 m tall. Its top edge is at the water surface. What is the total hydrostatic force on the gate? Use 9.81 kN/m^{3}.
examples.idea: The resultant force on a submerged plane surface is the pressure at the centroid of the area times the area. For a gate that reaches the surface the pressure diagram is a triangle, and the force acts at two thirds of the depth.
examples.steps:
Depth to centroid = 3.6 / 2 = 1.8 m, so pressure there = 9.81 × 1.8 = 17.66 kPa.

Area = 2.5 × 3.6 = 9 m^{2}.

F = 17.66 × 9 = 158.9 kN, acting 2.40 m below the surface.

examples.problem: A mercury manometer (specific gravity 13.6) connects two water pipes at the same elevation and shows a deflection of 0.25 m. What is the pressure difference between the pipes? Use 9.81 kN/m^{3} for water.
examples.idea: Work around the manometer from one pipe to the other, adding pressure going down and subtracting going up. The water columns on the two sides cancel except over the deflection, leaving (SG of mercury - 1) × specific weight of water × deflection.

examples.problem: A 1.5 m^{3} block with a specific gravity of 0.70 floats in water. What volume of the block is below the water surface?
examples.idea: Archimedes' principle: a floating body displaces a weight of fluid equal to its own weight. In water, the submerged fraction of the volume equals the body's specific gravity.
examples.steps: Weight of block = weight of displaced water, so submerged volume = SG × total volume = 0.70 × 1.5 = 1.050 m^{3}.

examples.problem: A tank holds 1.2 m of oil (specific gravity 0.82) floating on 1.8 m of water. What is the gauge pressure on the floor of the tank? Use 9.81 kN/m^{3} for water.
examples.idea: Pressure at depth is the sum of specific weight times thickness for each layer above. The lower layer starts from the pressure at the interface, not from zero.
examples.steps:
Pressure at the interface = 0.82(9.81)(1.2) = 9.65 kPa.

Add the water: 9.65 + 9.81(1.8) = 27.31 kPa.

examples.problem: A timber raft has a volume of 2.8 m^{3} and a specific gravity of 0.62. What is the largest cargo weight it can carry in fresh water before it is fully submerged?
examples.idea: At the limit the raft is fully submerged and displaces its whole volume of water. The buoyant force then equals the raft's weight plus the cargo, so the cargo is the weight of displaced water minus the weight of the raft.
examples.steps:
Buoyant force when submerged = 9.81(2.8) = 27.47 kN.

Raft weight = 0.62(9.81)(2.8) = 17.03 kN.

Cargo = 27.47 - 17.03 = 10.44 kN.

sections.deep:
In a fluid at rest, pressure depends only on depth: it rises by the specific weight for every unit of depth and is the same at any two points on the same level in the same connected fluid. That one rule solves manometers.

The force on a submerged plane surface is the pressure at the centroid of the area times the area. It acts below the centroid, at the centre of pressure, because pressure is larger lower down. Buoyancy is the net upward pressure force and equals the weight of the displaced fluid.
method: For a manometer, start at one end and move through the fluid: add specific weight × height going down, subtract going up.
For a plane surface, find the depth of the centroid and multiply the pressure there by the area.
Locate the centre of pressure with the handbook formula, or as the centroid of the pressure diagram.
For buoyancy, equate the weight of the body to the weight of displaced fluid.
State whether pressures are gauge or absolute.
sections.credit: Some of the points in this lesson follow Mark Mattson's 2022 FE review session for this topic, restated in this site's words.
sections.primer: In a fluid at rest, pressure depends only on depth: unit weight times depth. That pressure pushes at right angles on every surface it touches. An object in a fluid is pushed up by a force equal to the weight of the fluid it displaces.

terms: specific weight
weight per unit volume; for water 9.81 kN/m^{3} or 62.4 lb/ft^{3}
centroid
the geometric centre of an area, the point where it would balance if cut from uniform card
resultant
the single force that has the same effect as several forces acting together
moment
the turning effect of a force about a point: the force times its perpendicular distance from that point
specific gravity
density of a substance divided by the density of water; it has no units
symbols: depth of the centre of pressure
moment of inertia of the surface about its centroidal axis

sections.title: Energy, impulse and momentum
sections.body:
Three conservation laws solve most flow problems. Continuity: what flows in must flow out, so velocity rises where the pipe narrows. Energy: along a flow, pressure head, velocity head and elevation head add to a constant, less any losses. Momentum: a force is needed to change the speed or direction of a flow.

Add pump head as an energy gain and friction as a loss. Friction loss in pipes comes from the Darcy-Weisbach equation with a friction factor from the Moody diagram. The energy grade line shows total head; the hydraulic grade line sits below it by the velocity head.

formulas.name: Energy equation
formulas.expr: \frac{p_{1}}{specific weight} + \frac{V_{1}^{2}}{2g} + z_{1} + h_{pump} = \frac{p_{2}}{specific weight} + \frac{V_{2}^{2}}{2g} + z_{2} + h_{loss}

pitfalls: Forgetting that halving the diameter quarters the area and quadruples the velocity.
Putting a head loss on the wrong side of the energy equation.
Using p / density where the pressure head p / specific weight is needed.

example.problem: Water flows at 0.03 m^{3}/s through a 150 mm pipe. Find the velocity and the velocity head.

ideas.title: Use gauge pressure in the energy equation
ideas.text: Atmospheric pressure appears on both sides and cancels, so work in gauge pressure. An outlet open to the air is at zero. Put the datum at the lower point so one elevation term vanishes.

ideas.title: Thrust on a pipe bend
ideas.text: The pressure force p A acts along the pipe at each end of a bend. Because the two act in different directions they leave a resultant, 2 p A sin(angle / 2) when velocities are low, which a thrust block must resist. The block's bearing area is the thrust divided by the allowable soil pressure.

ideas.title: Continuity equation
ideas.text: Continuity for an incompressible fluid: the flow rate A V is the same at every section. Area scales with diameter squared, so velocity scales with the inverse square of the diameter ratio.

ideas.title: Bernoulli equation
ideas.text: Bernoulli's equation says pressure head + velocity head + elevation head stays constant along a streamline when there are no losses. In a horizontal pipe, a gain in velocity is paid for by a drop in pressure.

ideas.title: Impulse-momentum principle
ideas.text: The impulse-momentum principle: force equals the rate of change of momentum. The plate destroys all of the jet's momentum in the original direction, so F = (density)(Q)(V) = (density)(A)(V^{2}).

ideas.title: Darcy-Weisbach
ideas.text: The Darcy-Weisbach equation gives friction head loss as the friction factor times the length-to-diameter ratio times the velocity head: h_{f} = f (L/D)(V^{2}/2g).

ideas.title: Impulse-momentum principle
ideas.text: The momentum equation gives the force on the fluid as mass flow rate times the change in velocity. In the jet's original direction the velocity changes from V to V cos(angle), so the vane feels (density)(Q)(V)(1 - cos(angle)). A flat plate is the 90° case, and a full reversal at 180° doubles it.

ideas.title: Pipe bends
ideas.text: The pressure force p A acts along the pipe axis at each end of the bend. The two are equal in size but differ in direction, leaving a resultant of 2 p A sin(angle / 2) that a thrust block must resist.

examples.idea: Bernoulli's equation says pressure head + velocity head + elevation head stays constant along a streamline when there are no losses. In a horizontal pipe, a gain in velocity is paid for by a drop in pressure.

examples.problem: A 80 mm diameter water jet moving at 18 m/s strikes a flat plate at right angles. What force does the jet exert on the plate?
examples.idea: The impulse-momentum principle: force equals the rate of change of momentum. The plate destroys all of the jet's momentum in the original direction, so F = (density)(Q)(V) = (density)(A)(V^{2}).

sections.deep:
Three conservation laws solve flowing-fluid problems. Continuity conserves mass: flow rate Q = A V is constant along a pipe. The energy equation conserves energy: pressure head, velocity head and elevation head at one section, plus pump head, equal those at another plus turbine head and losses. The momentum equation relates forces to changes in the fluid's momentum and gives the forces on bends, nozzles and plates.

Friction loss in pipes follows the Darcy-Weisbach equation, with the friction factor from the Moody diagram, depending on Reynolds number and relative roughness. Minor losses are a coefficient times the velocity head.
method: Choose two sections where the most is known; a free surface has zero gauge pressure and negligible velocity.
Use continuity to relate the velocities.
Write the energy equation between the sections, including pump head and losses.
Solve for the unknown head, pressure or flow.
For forces, apply the momentum equation to a control volume with pressures and velocities at its faces.
sections.credit: Some of the points in this lesson follow Mark Mattson's 2022 FE review session for this topic, restated in this site's words.
sections.primer: Moving fluid carries energy in three forms: pressure, speed and height. Along a pipe or stream their total stays the same except for what friction takes away. Flow rate, velocity times area, stays constant, so a narrower section means faster flow.

terms: head
energy of a fluid expressed as a height of that fluid, in metres or feet
momentum
mass times velocity; a force acting for a time changes it
reynolds number
a ratio that tells whether flow is smooth (laminar, low values) or mixed and eddying (turbulent, high values)
resultant
the single force that has the same effect as several forces acting together
head loss
energy, expressed as a height of fluid, used up by friction and fittings
symbols: force in the direction of the incoming jet
